results.summary: This project implements a 6-bit ripple carry adder with a carry input and carry output, using continuous assignment without a clock. It takes two 6-bit numbers on the input and bidirectional pins and produces their sum on the output pins. The design is purely combinational and requires no external hardware. Silicon tests confirm that the adder works correctly, with one tester noting it works eventually.

This design implements an 8-bit vector compute-in-SRAM with eight multiply-and-add units and an adder tree that sums the results without precision loss. Weights and activations are programmed via operation codes, with weights remaining stationary for reuse. The design is tested through a Python test suite that covers individual MAC operations, weight loading, adder tree functionality, and readout, though most tests are commented out due to limited external signal access. It operates entirely within its own resources and does not interface with external hardware, though external signals might be needed to orchestrate multiple units with a control processor.

This project implements an 8-bit ripple carry adder that adds two 8-bit numbers using a cascade of full adders. The sum is output on the 8 output pins, and the design is purely combinational with no clock. It requires no external hardware, though switches and LEDs can be used for demonstration. Silicon tests confirm that the adder works correctly, with multiple testers verifying the sum of two 8-bit inputs.

This analog design models a quadratic integrate-and-fire (QIF) spiking neuron, where the output spikes and resets when the input voltage crosses a threshold. It is based on a published compact digital implementation and is intended for neuromorphic computing experiments. Testing involves applying an 8-bit digital signal and observing the spiking behavior, and it requires external hardware such as an ADLAM2000. The documentation is minimal, providing only a brief description and a reference to a lab manual.

This analog project implements an instrumentation amplifier for electrocardiogram signal acquisition, using a three-opamp array to extract low differential signals from noisy common-mode environments. The differential gain is digitally selectable via two input bits, providing 0 dB, 26 dB, or 46 dB gain, with a common-mode rejection ratio of 120 dB. Testing requires a balun, vector network analyzer, and power supplies to measure differential and common responses. The design includes a sense circuit to stabilize the analog ground and is intended for biomedical applications.

This SystemVerilog design implements a calculator that performs addition, AND, OR, and XOR operations on two input numbers, with the result displayed on a 4-digit Nixie tube display. It uses a 100 Hz clock and provides control signals for selecting numbers, positions, signs, and modes. Testing involves applying inputs and predicting the output to verify against the display. The design requires external Nixie tubes and associated driver hardware.

This analog project implements a Gilbert cell mixer for up and down conversion of signals, with both internal and external local oscillator options. The digital control part can generate internal LO signals at different frequencies or pass an external LO to the analog mixer. Testing requires biasing the input ports with 900-950 mV and applying a differential signal of about 20 mV peak-to-peak, typically using a custom interface PCB. Silicon tests confirm successful downconversion from 32 MHz RF and 30 MHz LO to a 2 MHz IF, and the author notes it works well with both internal and external LO sources.

This design reads run-length encoded video data from a QSPI flash memory and outputs it to a 640x480 VGA display, suitable for playing the Bad Apple music video. It requires external QSPI and VGA PMODs, and the SPI read latency is configurable via input pins. The design operates at 25.175 MHz and was successfully tested on silicon, playing Bad Apple, though there were minor issues with short back-to-back runs that the author believes are fixed in a later version.

This Verilog design generates phase-shifted PWM signals for controlling two PMOS and two NMOS transistors in a power converter, with configurable duty cycles and dead time to prevent cross-conduction. It includes a shift register for serial control, internal generation of phase-shifted triangular waveforms, and output multiplexing. The design operates at a 1000 Hz clock and requires no external hardware. Testing involves verifying the PWM outputs against the input duty cycles and control signals.

This design implements a ring-oscillator physically unclonable function (PUF) using reversible logic for fault tolerance, with 64 ring oscillators divided into two groups of 32. Challenges are generated by an LFSR, and responses are derived from frequency differences between selected oscillators, producing unique outputs per challenge. The design was tested on Vivado and OpenRoad, and requires no external hardware. It is notable for combining reversible logic with a PUF architecture to enhance security and fault tolerance.
